kurz: Four methods that condense a set of annual financial statements into one number answer four different questions, but none of them asks whether the share is cheap.

bloecke.md:
Four methods from four decades of capital market research condense a set of annual financial statements into a single number. They come from different authors and were estimated for different questions. If they are confused, you read statements into them that they do not make.

The F-score measures whether the financial position has improved compared with the previous year. The Z-score estimates how close a company is to insolvency. The M-score shows signs of aggressive accounting. The magic formula ranks shares by return on capital and price. It is the only one of the four methods that compares price with earning power, and even it only shows which of two shares offers relatively more earning power per euro of purchase price. The Z-score also contains the share price, but only through the market value of equity relative to liabilities.

All four are used for pre-selection. They do not replace a decision, but they save work, for example by selecting forty shares out of 600, which you then study more closely.

bloecke.titel: Four methods and the questions they address
bloecke.unter: On the left are the methods that only need the financial statements, on the right the methods that also use the share price and therefore fluctuate with it.

felder.text: Seven index variables and an accruals ratio from two consecutive sets of financial statements. Looks for traces of stretched accounting.
Four balance sheet ratios and the market value of equity. Estimates how close a company is to being unable to pay.
Nine yes-or-no tests, mostly against the previous year. Measures whether the balance sheet is improving.
Two rankings: return on capital and EBIT relative to enterprise value. Compares earning power per euro of purchase price.

bloecke.md:
## Piotroski's nine yes-or-no tests

The F-score goes back to an observation in the value segment. Shares with a high book-to-market ratio are cheap on average, but this segment contains many companies that are cheap for good reason. What was sought was a method that, within the segment, separates the companies that are recovering from those whose situation continues to deteriorate. It was to manage without a forecast and without a valuation model, using only the most recent and the previous financial statements.

The result is nine binary tests in three groups: four on profitability, three on leverage and liquidity and two on operating efficiency. Each test passed earns one point. 8 to 9 points are considered strong, 0 to 2 points weak. Five of the nine tests compare with the previous year, so the score mainly assesses the direction of development rather than the level reached.

bloecke.titel: The nine criteria for model company A (illustrative calculation, figures in €m)

bloecke.md:
Return on assets and asset turnover are based on the balance sheet total at the start of the year, the debt ratio on the average balance sheet total for the year. Model company A scores 7 out of 9 points. The two missing points are connected. The balance sheet total at the start of the year, on which asset turnover is based, grew from €800 million to €900 million, that is by 12.5%, whereas revenue grew only from €1,200 million to €1,300 million, that is by 8%. By the end of the year the balance sheet total rose further to €1,000 million, financed partly with 1.2 million new shares. Asset turnover falls because the capital tied up has grown faster than revenue. The score is meant to make such connections visible.

The F-score says nothing about the price of the share. A cyclical company that made a loss in the previous year and is now just in the black automatically collects points, because an improvement from a poor starting point also counts as an improvement. The F-score was intended as a second stage behind a valuation filter and never as a stand-alone strategy.

The F-score measures direction, the Z-score proximity to inability to pay, and the M-score how conspicuous the accounting is. None of them measures the value of a company. If a score is used as a buy signal, the question for which it was estimated has been swapped without anyone noticing.

## Altman's 1968 insolvency measure

In 1968 Altman estimated a linear discriminant function using 66 US industrial companies, half of which had become insolvent. The model consists of five weighted ratios and two thresholds. In the original study, two years before insolvency, it identified 72% of the later cases and gave a false alarm for 6% of the healthy firms.

The weights have been used unchanged since 1968. This gives rise to the first reservation. Coefficients from a sample of American industrial firms from the 1960s are applied today to the balance sheets of software and service companies of a kind that did not exist at the time.

bloecke.erklaerung: For listed industrial companies the following zones apply: above 2.99 unremarkable, 1.81 to 2.99 grey zone, below 1.81 distress zone.
bloecke.beispiel: Model company A: balance sheet total 1,000, working capital 160, retained earnings 210, EBIT 78, revenue 1,300, liabilities 570, market value 51.2 million shares at €12.00 = €614 million. This gives Z = 2.69.

bloecke.titel: Components of model company A's Z-score
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation. Almost half of the value comes from the revenue term, which is only indirectly related to the ability to pay.

bloecke.md:
The breakdown shows two properties. First, the revenue term alone contributes 1.30 of the 2.69 points. The model therefore systematically rates capital-intensive businesses with low asset turnover as more at risk, regardless of their financial position. Second, X4 contains the share price. If the share price halves to €6.00, the market value of equity falls to €307 million and the Z-score from 2.69 to around 2.37. The score then partly just confirms what the market has already priced in.

With German financial statements there is an additional problem of definition. X2 refers to cumulative retained earnings. In a balance sheet under the HGB (Commercial Code), these are spread across revenue reserves (Gewinnrücklagen, Section 266(3) A. III HGB), profit carryforward and distributable profit (Bilanzgewinn). If only the “revenue reserves” line is used, the score comes out systematically too low. In addition, since pension provisions count as liabilities on the balance sheet, an old pension commitment increases the denominator of X4 and lowers the score, even though it has little to do with current business risk.

For companies outside listed industry there are separate variants, such as the Z''-score without the revenue term: Z'' = 6.56 X1 + 3.26 X2 + 6.72 X3 + 1.05 X4. Here X4 uses the book value of equity, and the thresholds are 1.1 and 2.6. With values from a screener, you therefore need to know which variant is calculated there.

The Z-score was not estimated for banks, insurers and real estate companies, and the M-score is expressly not applicable to financial institutions. In addition, none of the scores is a legal concept. In Germany, grounds for insolvency are determined by inability to pay (Zahlungsunfähigkeit) under Section 17 of the Insolvency Code (InsO) and over-indebtedness (Überschuldung) with a going-concern forecast over twelve months (Section 19 InsO). The obligation to file for insolvency applies within three weeks in the case of inability to pay and within six weeks in the case of over-indebtedness (Section 15a InsO). A company can have a comfortable Z-score and still become unable to pay because it cannot meet a single payment when due.

## Beneish's M-score

The M-score checks whether a company's figures look unusual, and not whether the company is good. It compares two consecutive financial years and forms seven index variables, plus an accruals ratio. Five of the indices divide this year's value by last year's; for the margin index GMI and the depreciation index DEPI it is the other way round. For a company with no change at all, all seven indices are 1.

By far the largest weight is carried by TATA, that is net profit before extraordinary items minus operating cash flow, divided by the balance sheet total. This variable follows the same idea as Piotroski's fourth test, only as a continuous variable instead of a yes-or-no decision. Sloan described the same relationship in 1996 as the accrual anomaly. Profits that are not matched by an inflow of cash are, on average, less persistent.

bloecke.erklaerung: Values above -1.78 are considered conspicuous. The M-score is not applicable to financial institutions.
variablen: days' sales in receivables: receivables relative to revenue compared with the previous year
gross margin index: previous year's margin divided by the current margin
asset quality: share of assets outside current assets and property, plant and equipment
sales growth: revenue divided by the previous year's revenue
depreciation index: previous year's depreciation rate divided by the current one
selling and administrative expenses relative to revenue compared with the previous year
accruals: (net profit - operating cash flow) / balance sheet total
leverage index: debt ratio compared with the previous year
bloecke.beispiel: A company whose seven indices are exactly 1 and whose accruals are zero has M = -2.48. It is 0.70 points short of the threshold.

bloecke.titel: Contribution of each variable to the M-score (illustrative calculation)
zeilen: TATA accruals to balance sheet total

bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation. Model company B exceeds the threshold because days' sales in receivables, sales growth and accruals are all elevated at the same time, without any single value standing out as an outlier.

bloecke.md:
The calculation shows two things. First, the distance between the unremarkable company and the threshold is small. An accruals ratio of 15% of the balance sheet total is enough on its own to cross the threshold. Second, the conspicuousness of model company B arises from the sum of several values, none of which would be conspicuous on its own.

The most important limitation follows from the fact that genuine accounting manipulation is rare. Suppose one company in 200 manipulates, and the model additionally flags a few per cent of the unremarkable companies. Then the majority of hits are false, because there are so many more unremarkable companies. An M-score above -1.78 is therefore a reason for a closer examination. This includes reading the disclosures on revenue recognition in the notes, looking at the age structure of receivables and checking segment changes and transactions with related parties.

Each of the eight variables reflects a known pattern by which profits are brought forward or expenses deferred.

- DSRI rises when revenue is booked that nobody has paid for yet. It is the most reliable single signal of aggressive revenue recognition.
- A GMI above 1 means that the gross margin has fallen. A company under margin pressure has more reason to improve its figures through accounting policy.
- AQI measures how strongly the share of assets that belong neither to current assets nor to property, plant and equipment is growing. That is where capitalised costs are reported.
- SGI is not a feature of manipulation; it indicates pressure. Fast-growing companies are under pressure to meet expectations.
- A DEPI above 1 means that the depreciation rate has fallen, for example through extended useful lives.
- SGAI captures the opposite. Selling and administrative expenses that grow faster than revenue point to a deteriorating business.
- LVGI measures rising debt and thus the pressure from loan covenants.
- TATA is the most important variable. It measures the difference between reported profit and the inflow of cash.

## Greenblatt's magic formula

The magic formula reduces the selection to two ratios and a ranking. The earnings yield is EBIT divided by enterprise value, and the return on capital is EBIT divided by the sum of net working capital and net fixed assets. Both ratios start from EBIT and not from net profit, so that capital structure and tax rate do not distort the picture. The remaining steps are fixed and narrowly defined.

schritte.text: The minimum market capitalisation is typically above $50 million. Utilities, financials and ADRs are excluded because EBIT and invested capital are not comparable there.

One ranking is compiled by return on capital, one by earnings yield. The ranks are added together, and the lowest total comes first. A share ranked 40th and 60th is therefore ahead of one ranked 1st and 150th.
The portfolio comprises 20 to 30 shares, with two to three positions bought each month. This spreads the entry over the year instead of concentrating it on a single date.
Losing positions are sold one week before the anniversary, winning positions one week after it. This rule serves solely to optimise tax in the US and has nothing to do with the selection logic.

schritte.titel: Stick with it or do without
schritte.text: A set of rules is only a strategy if you also follow it in the years in which it lags behind the index.

bloecke.md:
In a German portfolio the fourth step is pointless, and annual turnover is expensive. For securities acquired after 2008, there is no longer a holding period after which price gains would become tax-free. Capital gains are taxable regardless of the holding period (Section 20(2) sentence 1 no. 1 EStG, Income Tax Act) and are taxed at 25% plus the solidarity surcharge, 26.375% in total (Section 32d(1) EStG). The saver's allowance (Sparer-Pauschbetrag) of €1,000 per person (Section 20(9) EStG) covers only a little if the portfolio is turned over completely every year.

In addition there is the separate pot for share losses. Losses from the sale of shares may only be offset against gains from the sale of shares (Section 20(6) sentence 4 EStG). An investor who systematically sells the losers every year collects losses in a pot that can only be reduced by gains on shares. With individual shares, the gains at least fall into the same category, but in a mixed portfolio of ETFs and individual shares the rule acts as a real barrier.

bloecke.titel: Final wealth with and without annual switching
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation with €10,000, a gross return of 8% a year and 26.375% tax on realised gains. The saver's allowance, church tax and trading costs are not taken into account.

serien.name: held, taxed only at the end

bloecke.md:
After twenty years, final wealth with annual switching is around 15% below that of the portfolio that was held, even though not a single investment decision was worse. A mechanical strategy first has to make up this gap before it can perform better at all.

## Empirical findings

Piotroski examined the years 1976 to 1996. He reports that the average return in the segment with high book-to-market ratios could be raised by at least 7.5 percentage points a year by restricting the selection to high F-scores. The effect was concentrated in small and medium-sized companies with little analyst coverage and thin trading, that is, in the area where implementation is most expensive.

For the magic formula there is an independent evaluation covering 2003 to 2015. It found 11.4% a year compared with 8.7% for the S&P 500, with considerably higher volatility and several years of underperformance between 2007 and 2011. Greenblatt's own backtest figures from the book are not considered here because they have not been independently verified.

There is also a general finding that applies to every published rule. In 2016 McLean and Pontiff showed for 97 documented return patterns that the excess return declines by around 58% on average after publication. Investors who implement a rule from a book that millions of people have read should therefore not count on the figures from the book.

- Valuation comes first, then the F-score as a quality filter, and finally the Z-score and M-score as exclusion criteria. In the reverse order, you sort by ratios and justify the valuation afterwards.
- Check the definitions. Screeners calculate the same scores differently, for example with the balance sheet total at the start of the year or on average, with EBIT with or without special items, as Z or Z''. Two providers can easily give two different values for the same company.
- Comparisons are best made within the sector. A Z-score of 2.4 means something different in retail than in plant engineering.
- You can look up financial statements yourself. German incorporated companies must disclose them (Section 325 HGB), and they are available via the Company Register (Unternehmensregister).

mitnehmen: The F-score, Z-score and M-score answer three different questions, about direction, proximity to insolvency and conspicuousness, but none of them asks whether a share is cheap.
Through X4 the Z-score contains the share price and through X5 asset turnover, so it reacts to falling share prices and penalises capital-intensive businesses regardless of their ability to pay.
Because genuine accounting manipulation is rare, most M-score hits are false alarms, and a conspicuous value justifies an examination but not yet a verdict.

With mechanical strategies involving annual turnover, 26.375% tax on realised gains falls due immediately in Germany, and share losses are subject to the separate pot under Section 20(6) sentence 4 EStG.
The excess return of published return patterns declines by around 58% on average after publication, so historical backtest figures are not an expected return.

begriffe.text: Score from 0 to 9 based on nine binary tests of profitability, leverage, liquidity and efficiency. Five of the tests compare with the previous year. The score measures improvement and is not a valuation.

Weighted sum of five ratios for estimating how close listed industrial companies are to insolvency, not intended for banks, insurers and real estate companies. Values above 2.99 are considered unremarkable, 1.81 to 2.99 a grey zone, and anything below that a distress zone.

Weighted sum of seven year-on-year indices and an accruals ratio, intended to indicate aggressive accounting. Values above −1.78 are considered conspicuous. The score is a screening signal and not proof; it is not applicable to financial institutions.

Difference between reported profit and operating cash flow, usually relative to the balance sheet total. High accruals mean profit without an inflow of cash and are empirically associated with weaker subsequent results.

Selection rule by Joel Greenblatt. Shares are ranked separately by return on capital and by earnings yield (EBIT/enterprise value), and the ranks are then added together. 20 to 30 shares are held and replaced annually; financials and utilities are excluded.
